linkage.caveat: Rates describe trials that posted a usable result. A trial counted as having no identified publication may still be published; matching has false negatives.

publication_model.note: Outcome is whether a publication was identified. A positive log_hr coefficient means trials with weaker treatment effects were MORE likely to be linked to a publication; a negative one means they were less likely. Small cohorts give wide intervals -- read the interval, not the point estimate.

priors.interpretation: Adding 20 registry-only trial(s) moved the pooled hazard ratio toward the null (from 0.761 to 0.796). In this cohort the identified literature shows a larger treatment effect than the registry record as a whole.
priors.caveat: This compares only results that are observable. Trials with neither a publication nor a posted result are not included here; their influence is explored through sensitivity analysis instead.

rows.label: Your assumption
rows.note: The design as proposed, by construction hitting its power target.

consequence.summary: A trial sized for HR 0.65 needs 170 events. If the registry-aware estimate of HR 0.80 is closer to the truth, those 170 events deliver 32% power rather than 80%, and reaching the target would take 606 events (+436 more).

design.method: Schoenfeld approximation for the log-rank test, 1:1 allocation. Event counts drive the calculation; participant counts appear only when an overall event probability is supplied.

sensitivity.note: Each of the 316 trial(s) with no identified publication and no posted result is represented by one pseudo-trial at the assumed hazard ratio, given the median precision of the 84 trial(s) that did report. These are assumptions under test, not findings.

backtest.verdict: At a target of 80%, literature-only covered 81% and registry-aware covered 79%. Mean absolute error on log(HR) was 0.278 versus 0.267. Literature-only predicted a stronger effect than the held-out trials delivered (bias -0.036 on log(HR)); registry-aware was closer to unbiased (+0.010). That direction is what publication selection predicts. The two models traded off: one was better calibrated, the other more accurate. This cohort does not settle the question. With a cohort this size, a few folds move these numbers materially; treat the comparison as indicative rather than conclusive.
backtest.method: Leave-one-out. Each held-out trial is predicted from a random-effects pool of the remaining trials, using a prediction interval for the next trial rather than a confidence interval for the mean.

guardrails: A trial with no identified publication is not necessarily unpublished; matching has false negatives.
A trial with no identified publication is not assumed to be null. Its influence is explored through sensitivity analysis.
Registered-versus-published differences are described, never characterized as misconduct.
Only hazard ratios for one endpoint class are pooled; other effect measures are excluded rather than converted.
